PUBLISHERS NOTE

The late Mr. Simon Alexander Hewavitarane, who during his lifetime had begun to publish the Tripitaka, left a bequest for its completion after his death. He died suddenly on 17th January 1913, and in accordance with his wishes, his Trustees published the Commentaries on the Text in 49 volumes. After seventy years, these books are no longer readily available.

His widow, Mrs. Somawati Hewavitarane, who passed away on 10th January 1982 at the age of 94, had prior to her death established the Somawati Hewavitarane Trust to carry on the good work started by her late husband, and bequeathed her entire estate to this Trust.

We, the Trustees of the Somawati Hewavitarane Trust, having recognized the need to reprint the Commentaries, have undertaken this task to assist both students and teachers of the Dhamma. We hope that this act will help preserve the Noble Teachings of the Blessed One for the benefit of future generations, and thereby prolong the life of the Buddha Sasana for many more thousands of years.

May the fruits of this meritorious act benefit the late Simon Alexander Hewavitarane and Somawati Hewavitarane, Great Lay Devotee, throughout Samsara and toward their final attainment of Nibbana.

PREFATORY NOTE.

With the publication of the Sāratthasamuccaya or Catubhānavāraṭṭhakathā, I have much pleasure in placing before the public the 27th Volume of the Simon Hewavitarne Bequest Series. The editing of this volume has been done by the Venerable Doranegoda Pandita Nanasena Thero, Principal of the Vidyaraja Pirivena and member of the Tripitaka Publication Committee.

The proofs have been revised by the Venerable Kodagoda Upasena Maha Thero, Adhikarana Nayaka of the Ramañña Sect, Principal of Sri Saddharmodaya Pirivena, Panadura.

This Commentary appears to be a handbook compiled from the existing Commentaries of Buddhaghosa and Dhammapala, and adapted for use in this country by novices entering the monastic order. The author was a pupil of the Venerable Ananda Vanaratana Maha Thero of the Maha Vihara tradition, but his name is not known. A similar work is the Suttasangaha Commentary.

I am pleased to announce that the Samantapasadika Vinaya Commentary is ready for publication and will be released soon.

I wish to convey my heartfelt thanks to the Reverend Editor.

S. K. Moonesinghe.

PREFACE.

Like the pollen-circle of the sun, the Buddha, the great teacher who dispelled darkness, shines forth with the light of liberation — may this book, the essence of liberation, be rendered pure.

What is this called the Sārattha-samuccaya, the four-section explanatory commentary?

Answer: The commentary (atthakathā) here is that which accompanies the text, proceeding along with it, offering miscellaneous teachings here and there. That which was composed with the skill of twenty-two teachers, following the method of all languages taught together, was established here in Sinhala, in the Sinhala language, by one knowledgeable in the analytical method. It was written in the manner of exposition for the benefit of those who study the Buddha's teaching, by the Elder Dīpankara of Vāsi. Through this, the Sinhala people were enabled to understand. For indeed, the Elder of Buddhist learning had formerly composed in Sinhala a comprehensive exposition of the entire scripture. Some able persons commended it. Then, as time passed, it became scarce. The great Abhayasīlā assembly of practitioners declared: "It is not proper that this important Sinhala text should be unavailable — it should be reprinted." This itself was the basis for the matter. For the purpose of making basic commentary available, this work has been published. The Elder of Buddhist learning personally checked and corrected the text. Therefore it should be known: everything needed for the advancement of the Dhamma is provided herein. In this manner the publication has been prepared and released.

What is the purpose of this edition?

Answer: At the present time, the monastic community, beginning with the most senior pupils, teachers, and learned scholars, along with lay supporters, have an interest in Dhamma texts. Among them, some have shown readiness to study carefully. Thus the interest in Dhamma texts has grown. The measure of this is seen in the way the Dhamma is studied and practiced by all — thus it is said throughout.

He who is the venerable Hewavitarana Mahashaya, bearer of the entire Tipitaka, having kept alive the glory of the teaching without interruption — the one who fulfilled the wishes of those in the world — the custodian of the Tipitaka manuscripts, the chief patron C. J. Hewavitarana Mahashaya, through the merit he had accumulated, in the fifty-eighth year, caused the fundamental texts of the brotherhood of elders to be published and set forth. Through effort and dedication, having fulfilled the great wish, he accomplished what was dear to his heart. Did Mara the evil one, who hinders the dispensation, try to obstruct? Those great brotherhood of elders, having overcome all those hindrances and obstacles, attained their goal. Having accomplished this through the Tipitaka treasury, making it available for study, through the great Dhamma treasury — may the Triple Gem protect all, be it so, truly.

That the Tipitaka may be studied in the monastery,
Written with one's own hand with clear mindfulness,
That it may protect the people in all directions —
May it be so through the grace of Hewavitarana.

The names of the Nikaya-compendiums are as follows:

"The Digha, Majjhima, Samyutta, and the Abhidhamma collection —
these five Nikayas constitute the Dhamma in its entirety."

The discourses of the Digha Nikaya are the long discourses; the Majjhima Nikaya consists of the middle-length discourses; the Samyutta Nikaya consists of the connected discourses grouped by topic; the Anguttara Nikaya consists of discourses arranged numerically in increasing order.

The Khuddakapatha, Dhammapada, Udana, Itivuttaka, Suttanipata, Vimanavatthu, Theragatha, Therigatha, Jataka, Niddesa, Patisambhida, Apadana, Buddhavamsa, Cariyapitaka, and the Vinayapitaka and Abhidhammapitaka — all the remainder beyond the four Nikayas is called the Khuddaka Nikaya.

Sārattha-samuccaya

Why is it called the "Buddhas' Assembly" (Buddhānikāya)? Because it is the dwelling-place and gathering of many Buddhas assembled together, and because of that assembled dwelling it is called a nikāya (collection/assembly).

"Even in a single assembly I do not perceive any sound, just as creatures go in search of livelihood" — in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, the Vikallanikāya, and so on, such terms appear in the world in connection with the Teaching.

Now the Going for Refuge, the Ten Training Rules, the qualities of a novice — associated with the Ratana Sutta, the Kāraṇīya-metta Sutta, and related texts — have been placed here under the heading of the Buddhakkhanda. They are arranged with the Metta Sutta and related texts: the Metta Sutta comes under the heading of the Theragāthā-nikāya; and from the Saṃyutta Nikāya comes the Isigili Sutta; from the Dīgha Nikāya the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta is drawn. These suttas having been cited from their respective nikāyas, the Isigili Sutta is taken for reference. In this same way the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta, the Metta Sutta, the Dhaja Sutta, and the Ratana Sutta — by means of these, it is said, recitation should be performed.

This having been arranged, in order to show the sequence of these selected suttas, I now take up the explanation, beginning with the phrase: "I go for refuge to the Buddha — and so forth — I go for refuge."

The summary matrix of topics in the following section is:

Why and by whom was this Going for Refuge spoken?
Why was it spoken as it was, and why in this particular order from the beginning?

Having clarified the basis and the preliminary matter up to that point,
let one illuminate the meaning of Going for Refuge to the Buddha.

Let one illuminate each cause and condition point by point,
and the method of the Dhamma refuge — that is the approach here.

Let one indicate the reasons with precision,
and illuminate the Going for Refuge with similes.

Now first of all, regarding this Going for Refuge — by whom was it spoken, how was it spoken, where was it spoken, when was it spoken, and why was it spoken thus, and from what beginning? Let us examine this carefully. As to who spoke it — was it spoken by the Blessed One? Yes, it was spoken by the Blessed One, not by a disciple, not by a seer, not by a god. Where? At Isipatana in the Deer Park at Bārāṇasī. For what purpose? Because those companions who had previously been with the Blessed One...

Saranavannana (Commentary on the Refuges)

For the welfare of many, for the happiness of the world, the Dhamma is being taught by the One worthy of offerings. What is comparable? Those who have gone forth and those who have received higher ordination, as follows: "Thus, monks, having taught the teaching, having given full ordination, having first addressed them with words of good counsel, having caused them to sit at the feet of monks, having had them learn by heart — in this way, having been thus instructed, they go to the Buddha for refuge, to the Dhamma for refuge, to the Sangha for refuge."

Why is it called the "Kassamo" etc.? In this ninefold training, as found in the three Pitakas among the sacred texts, as set forth by the noble ones of old, gods and humans become lay followers or those who have gone forth, and thus the teaching supports them. In the origin story relating to the Buddhas, this has been stated at the beginning — this is the explanation of that beginning. What does "hidananokkhana" mean? What has now been stated as "Taking refuge in the Excellent One, in the community" — this too is without a further basis. Having crossed beyond the floods of passion, having attained liberation of mind, and being free from the cycle of existence, those who are truly established in the teaching are led to the cessation of suffering. Thus the Buddha — the Awakened One — the Blessed One...

[Page 8 of the Sāratthasamuccaya]

Now, in order to illuminate the Three Refuges as stated with similes, the text proceeds: "In this manner — like the full moon risen, so is the Buddha; like the radiance of the full moon diffused, so is the Dhamma; like the world illuminated by the light of the full moon, so is the Sangha. Like the morning sun, with its net of rays spreading everywhere, so is the Buddha; like its rays, so is the Dhamma; like the world illuminated by it, so is the Sangha. Like a man who clears a great forest — clearing away the forest of defilements, so is the Buddha; like the clearing away of that forest, so is the Dhamma; like those who dwell freed from that forest of defilements, so is the Sangha. Like a great physician — so is the Buddha; like his pleasant remedy, so is the Dhamma; like those freed of sickness who live in health, so is the Sangha. Like an arrow-remover — so is the Buddha; like the removal of the arrow, so is the Dhamma; like one whose arrow is removed, so is the Sangha. Like one who destroys the arising of delusion — so is the Buddha, like the means of destroying it so is the Dhamma, like the world freed from the flood of delusion, so is the Sangha. Like a skilled physician who removes the disease of defilements from the world — so is the Buddha; like those afflicted with that disease of defilements, so is the Sangha. Like a great ship — so is the Buddha; like a fine vessel, so is the Dhamma; like those ferried to the further shore, so is the Sangha. Like a great mountain — so is the Buddha; like one freed from sickness, so is the Dhamma; like those who dwell in health, so is the Sangha. Like a lamp — so is the Buddha; like the light it gives, so is the Dhamma; like those who walk by that light, so is the Sangha. Like a jewel mine — so is the Buddha; like the jewels it contains, so is the Dhamma; like those enriched by those jewels, so is the Sangha."

Like the Sarula, so the Buddha shines; like the lion's water, so the Dhamma; like the prince of the noble clan, so the noble Sangha. One should recollect the Dhamma. Why so? Because from the well-proclaimed (svākkhāto) quality onward, the Dhamma — as taught through precepts and so forth — even to a householder provides a basis. And so through the recollection of the Dhamma, it is not divided; and compared to the Dhamma of the world, it is superior. The well-proclaimed Dhamma, as summarized from beginning through its entirety, is complete and not deficient, and fully practiced leads to liberation from defilements. Unlike the teachings of the world which are subject to distortion: these teachings of the world are near to distortion, while the Dhamma here — through these gradual trainings — maintains its character without distortion and without confusion.

The Dhamma of the world, on the other hand, suited to nibbāna in its own nature, being completely practiced through the path that leads to nibbāna, and through the stages of attainment, through the full training — the well-proclaimed Dhamma (svākkhāto) is distinguished. Nibbāna, being calmly and moderately described in its character, is visible here and now (sandiṭṭhiko) as something that the Noble One realizes personally, is directly visible, not delayed, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise each for themselves. So too, one who has right view (sammādiṭṭhi) achieves it for themselves by their own effort in this very world. Thus this Dhamma, being seen and understood, is a cause for confidence. And so the one who has attained right view (sammādiṭṭhika), attaining it thus, verifying it in successive stages, attains it again and again through right view, attains the seen and verifiable, and so the Dhamma is confirmed as directly visible and well-attained.

The supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma), through the occasion of meditation-attainment and through the occasion of functional activity, makes itself apparent in this way. For Nibbana is such that, just as that Arahant who has seen it directly sees it as directly visible (sanditthika). Therefore, in one respect, it is "not a matter of time" (akalika) — not something belonging to a particular time in the sense of waiting for a season to bear fruit in a later existence; rather, in the sense that when one practices, the fruit arises right then and there, in that very moment. But in another sense, one might ask: what is "timely" (kalika)? That is the wholesome Dhamma (kusala-dhamma) of the mundane world. For ordinary good deeds, unlike supramundane ones, are indeed timely — they ripen in a future time and place. This has been stated here as an example. Moreover, because the supramundane Dhamma does not belong to the category of "timely" things such as pleasant and unpleasant seasonal experiences, it is therefore called "akalika" (timeless).

Now, one may ask: in how many ways is the Arahant's quality to be seen and known directly? Because of knowledge and purity — just as gold that is pure and free of dross is fit to be fashioned into whatever form, so too this Dhamma: why? Because of the absence of ignorance. Just as when ignorance is removed and knowledge stands firm, like the sky cleared of clouds, filled with the full moon's light — the wise one who is pure and cleansed: thus, because of knowledge and because of purity, the Arahant's quality is to be seen in both these ways. Regarding "Opanayika" (leading inward): it means "leading toward" — from the time of its arising, through the practice of meditation, it continuously leads the practitioner forward, drawing him ever closer. In this way, the supramundane Dhamma leads inward to Nibbana. It is "opanayika" in the sense that through functional activity it draws one to liberation, to the Arahant state. Regarding the characteristic of "fully attaining the enlightenment factor of concentration" — the phrase "at whatever time the mind is uplifted" means: "at that time, the enlightenment factor of tranquility should be developed." Regarding the enlightenment factor of concentration — the phrase "at whatever time the mind is uplifted" means "at that time the enlightenment factor of concentration should be developed." Regarding the enlightenment factor of equanimity — "at whatever time the mind is uplifted, at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity should be developed" — thus it is stated. "Developed" means: bringing unarisen equanimity to arise, and fulfilling the development of what has arisen.

These seven enlightenment factors, when developed, lead to the attainment of arahantship. Just as the wheel-treasure, foremost among the treasures of the wheel-turning monarch, rolls through many levels of existence and illuminates the path — so too does the Dhamma-body, like the jewel-treasure that lights up the darkness — so too does the energy-enlightenment factor, like the elephant-treasure that leads the way — so too does the rapture-enlightenment factor, like the wish-fulfilling gem that illuminates with inner light — so too does the tranquility-enlightenment factor, like the woman-treasure that brings peace and comfort — so too does the concentration-enlightenment factor, like the householder-treasure that brings beings together in harmony — and thus all these are comparable to the treasures of the wheel-turning king.
